match.reason: None of the bank points teaches that a text's reputation is praised or criticised on first appearance and judged differently later; the closest ones cover readers' changing values and context, which is related but not the same idea of reception and critical reputation over time.

note:
A fresh check found these problems in this version. Fix each one, and keep everything that is right:
- Card, fact: The card states flatly that 'the words of the text stay the same'. Texts are sometimes revised or edited after publication, for example later editions or the 2023 edits to Roald Dahl's books. A qualifier such as 'usually' or 'in most cases' would avoid teaching an absolute that is not always true. The why for (a) relies on the same absolute claim.

rejected.title: How a text's reputation changes
card: A text's reputation is how it is judged by readers and critics. It can be praised or criticised when it first appears.
Later readers can judge the same text differently. A text once ignored may be praised, and a text once admired may be questioned.
The words of the text stay the same, so the text itself has not got better or worse. What changes is the readers: their values, their world and the questions they ask.
To explain a change in reputation, ask what the first audience valued and what later audiences value. Then link that difference to how each judged the text.
rejected.remember: The text stays the same. Its reputation moves with the readers who judge it.

a.q: Lena wants to explain why a novel mocked by critics in 1930 is praised today. What should she do first?
opts: Compare what readers valued in 1930 and what they value now
Find the parts of the novel that were rewritten after 1930
Decide whether the 1930 critics were poor judges of writing
Check whether the novel has improved as it has aged
a.why: A change in reputation comes from the readers, so Lena should compare what each audience valued and link that to their judgements. Looking for rewritten parts or an improved novel is tempting but wrong, because the words of the text stay the same.
a.clue: Which has changed since 1930: the novel or the people reading it?

b.q: In 1950, a play about a young woman who leaves her family to work in the city was criticised as improper. Audiences today praise it as bold. Which comment best explains the shift?
opts: Today's audiences value women's independence more
The play was changed to suit audiences today
Audiences in 1950 disliked all plays about cities
The play has become better written since 1950
b.why: The change comes from what each audience valued: 1950 audiences judged the woman's choice by their own values, and today's audiences judge it by different ones. The option about better writing is tempting but wrong, because the text itself has not changed.
b.clue: Compare what each audience valued, not the play itself.

a.q: A novel was mocked by critics when it was published in 1930. Readers today praise it. What best explains the change?
opts: Readers' values and contexts have changed
The words of the novel have been rewritten
Critics in 1930 had not read the novel
Praise is always given to older texts
a.why: The text is the same, but later readers bring different values and a different world to it. The tempting option about rewriting is wrong because the card says the words stay the same.
a.clue: Ask who has changed: the text or its readers?
